title: Achieving Equilibrium Under Utility Heterogeneity: An Agent-Attention Framework for Multi-Agent Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning
headline: Open finding: Unobserved independently distributed opponent utility preferences make the classical Bayesian Nash equilibrium best-response construction undefined or inapplicable without access to global realized preferences.

work.title: Achieving Equilibrium Under Utility Heterogeneity: An Agent-Attention Framework for Multi-Agent Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning
work.venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence

claims.label: Theorem 1 / Appendix Theorem 4
claims.gist: Unobserved independently distributed opponent utility preferences make the classical Bayesian Nash equilibrium best-response construction undefined or inapplicable without access to global realized preferences.
claims.statement: Unobserved independently distributed opponent utility preferences make the classical Bayesian Nash equilibrium best-response construction undefined or inapplicable without access to global realized preferences.
conditions: Agents observe their own preferences but not opponents' independently distributed preferences.
Behavioral strategies are measurable on each player's own type space.
claims.quantifiers: The theorem's categorical claim for the stated hidden-preference setting.

result.summary: The proof imposes the wrong measurability requirement; an explicit threshold strategy is a measurable pure BNE under hidden independent preference types.
result.witness: The proof imposes the wrong measurability requirement; an explicit threshold strategy is a measurable pure BNE under hidden independent preference types.
result.argument: Source lock, sigma-algebra audit, explicit two-player measurable BNE, POMOMDP embedding and rescue attempts. Limits: Does not establish universal BNE existence or challenge the empirical architecture and results.
not_claimed: The counterexample defeats the categorical impossibility claim, not all hidden-preference learning difficulties.
